newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia readies for polls amid mounting dissent.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia readies for polls amid mounting dissent.

text.p: Indonesia on Tuesday entered the final run-up to general elections this week after a campaign marked by the worst political violence in over three decades and growing dissent against the rule of President Suharto.
But none of this was likely to stop the ruling Golkar party from maintaining its tight grip on the country.
Political analysts said they expected Golkar to sweep back to power in Thursday's balloting, in which 125 million people in the world's fourth-most populous nation are eligible to vote.

Hundreds of thousands of party supporters took to the streets in Jakarta and elsewhere during the campaign in what some analysts said was a spontaneous explosion of partisanship and youthful exuberance, as well as frustration with a system which allows political demonstrations for only a month every five years.
There were frequent clashes between supporters of Golkar and the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP), which is one of the two minority parties permitted to contest the elections.
"I haven't seen such intense anger, jealousy and frustration before," political commentator Mochtar Buchori told Reuters.
The campaign culminated in the death of at least 142 people in the city of Banjarmasin on Borneo island after rioting and arson last Friday following clashes between Golkar and PPP supporters.
Most of those killed were people trapped by a fire which broke out in a shopping plaza which they were ransacking.

The government-run electoral commission imposed a five-day cooling off period between the end of campaigning on Friday and the actual voting, and there have been no reports of fresh trouble since Banjarmasin.

Indonesia's general elections are usually mainly ritual affairs, with Golkar's victory assured. The government clamps down on dissent, and there were further signs on Tuesday that nothing has changed this year.

The Jakarta Post, the country's top English-language daily, reported that former PPP legislator Sri Bintang Pamungkas, who is serving a four-year prison sentence on charges of defaming Suharto, had been sacked from his job as a lecturer at a state-run university.
The newspaper also said another politician had been accused in a Jakarta court on Monday of slandering Suharto and faced a prison sentence of up to six years.

Separately, the newspaper reported that a group of people had alleged in a lawsuit they had been paid by deputy parliament speaker Surjadi to evict loyalists of Megawati Sukarnoputri, the country's best-known opposition figure, from the headquarters of the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) last year.
Megawati, the daughter of late founding president Sukarno and a critic of the Suharto regime, was ousted from the PDI leadership by Surjadi in June 1996 in an act which was blessed by the government.
The eviction of Megawati loyalists from the PDI headquarters a month later triggered the worst rioting seen in Jakarta for two decades.
Surjadi was not immediately available for comment on the lawsuit, which alleges he still owes money to the group which helped in the eviction.
The government has said the Surjadi faction represents the genuine PDI, the third party eligible to contest elections, and has barred Megawati and her supporters from participating.
Golkar set a target of 70.02 percent of the vote, compared to the 68 percent it won in the last elections in 1992. The PPP won 17 percent in 1992 and the PDI 15 percent.

Analysts said that since the result was a foregone conclusion, key issues which will be watched included the percentages gained by the three parties and the size of the so-called Golput, or White Party -- a reference to people who spoil their ballots or abstain as a mark of protest.
Golkar officials put the size of Golput between three and four percent in the 1992 elections, in which about 90 percent of the electorate cast their ballots.
